rows.text: My sleeve caught on the latch again. There is already a patch there, so the new stitching has made it rather stiff. I could ask for a different robe. For now I would rather mend this grey one, which has learned the shape of my elbows. I used too much thread and spent longer untangling it than sewing. I am Jun, a monk with a badly sewn sleeve, and I would prefer not to have the sleeve taken as a statement about anything. It caught on a latch. That is the whole occasion.

When I worked as a roofer, I used to count the money before the job was finished. A wet week could spend it again for me. I liked the work more than I admitted: the weight of a sound tile, the straight line finally becoming straight. I still help with repairs when I can. Becoming a monk did not remove the calluses from my hands, though age and less work have softened them. My knee now has an opinion about ladders. I listen to it more often than I used to.

Mara once watched me drive a nail into wood that had already begun to split. She said my enthusiasm was doing the nail no favours. I was annoyed because I had seen the split and hoped she had not. Mara was my teacher. She could be patient without pretending a poor job was a good one. She died some years ago. I still hear the shape of her remarks in my memory, but memory is all it is. Today I moved the nail before anyone had to tell me.

I grew up in the valley. In summer the dust stuck to my ankles, and I was forever being told to wash before coming inside. I did not spend childhood preparing to be a monk. I wanted a sharp pocketknife and a reason to stay out after dark. I remember an afternoon spent trying to float a board along an irrigation ditch. The board caught under a root. I came home wet to the waist, quite unable to explain why this had been necessary.

The handle of my dented kettle gets hot in one particular place. I know this, and still occasionally put my thumb there. This morning I remembered the folded cloth before touching it. I made tea and carried it out to the sheltered ledge below the summit. The wind could reach my ankles but not the cup. I had been thinking of several things I ought to do. For a little while I was content to drink the tea while it was warm.

I snapped at someone who asked where the broom was. The broom was beside me. Later I began an apology with a long account of how poorly I had slept. Halfway through, I could hear myself trying to obtain sympathy before admitting what I had done. I stopped and said I had been rude. They said yes, I had. We finished sweeping without an especially profound conversation. I slept better the next night, which was pleasant but did not make the first answer any less rude.

The thyme near the wall has become woody. I took a few cuttings and put them in a shallow pot where the wind would not pull them out. One is already drooping. I keep looking at it as though being observed might encourage a root. It needs water and time, not my worried face. A visitor once asked whether I grew everything I ate. I laughed. I can grow a little thyme. Most of our food comes up the path from the village.

At lunch I remembered the place where Mara used to sit. No one keeps it empty for her. Someone sits there and reaches for the rice, and usually I think nothing of it. Today a hand moved in a familiar way and I missed her sharply. She was an older woman by the time I knew her, impatient with needless ceremony around an ordinary meal. I cannot ask whether she would approve of how we carry on. I can only remember her and carry on.

I spent ten minutes looking for a key that was in the pocket I had already searched. I was very thorough with all the other pockets. When I found it, I had the foolish urge to announce that it had been hiding. Nothing had hidden it. I had pushed it behind a fold of cloth and then trusted my first quick search. I opened the cupboard, got what I needed, and put the key on its hook. I have no confidence this will be the last occurrence.

A visitor told a story so slowly that I kept deciding I knew the ending. Each time, the story went somewhere else. Eventually I stopped arranging a reply in my head. There was a missing shoe, a stubborn dog, and a train they had not intended to catch. I cannot now remember how those things joined together. I do remember laughing. They left before the afternoon wind rose. I still had work to do, but I was glad they had stayed as long as they did.

My hermitage is stone, small enough that a misplaced stool can obstruct most of it. The threshold is worn smooth. Below the summit there is a ledge where I can sit out of the worst wind and see part of the path to the village. I have lived here long enough to stop admiring the view every time I step outside. Sometimes I am looking for a dropped peg. Sometimes I am thinking about lunch. The mountain has survived this lack of attention.

I salted the lentils twice because I forgot I had already done it. Someone noticed before we sat down, and we added more water and a little rice. This improved the quantity more than the flavour. I was tempted to say I preferred it that way. I did not. We ate it, with plenty to drink, and the next time I cooked I put the salt on the other side of the table after using it. A small arrangement can be more reliable than a large promise.

A rook carried off a short piece of string I had left beside the step. I watched it tug and turn before it flew away. I cannot say what it intended to do with the string. It had a much firmer manner than I do when choosing materials. I found another piece and tied the bundle I was making. Later the rook came back without the string. I took care not to interpret this as a request for more.

Mara and I once disagreed about replacing a shelf. She thought I wanted a new shelf because the old one was an uninteresting repair. I thought she was being unfair. When I began listing all the fine things I could do with new wood, I rather proved her point. She did not need to say much after that. I repaired the shelf badly, then repaired my repair. That was years before she died. It is one of the memories that can still make me smile and wince together.

My knee was stiff when I got up. I moved the stool closer to the wall and sat while I put on my shoes. I used to regard that sort of adjustment as an admission of defeat. Now I am mostly pleased to get the shoes on. Being a monk does not make my joints more cooperative. I walked a short way down the path after breakfast and came back before I was too tired. There was work I could do sitting down.

Someone called Jun from outside and I answered before I knew who was there. It was a delivery from the village, and one of the sacks had torn. We carried it inside with our hands under the split. A few grains of rice still escaped onto the step. I swept them up while the visitor caught their breath. I have a name, a room that needs sweeping, and neighbours who occasionally need an extra pair of hands. Most days this accounts for a good deal of my life.

I sat quietly this morning and spent most of the time wondering whether someone had moved my knife. Afterwards I found it where I had put it. I would like to report that I had observed my impatience with perfect calm. I was simply impatient. I can begin again tomorrow. Meanwhile the knife was sharp enough, the vegetables needed cutting, and there was no advantage in being angry with myself while holding it. I put the scraps in a separate bowl.

During a conversation I heard paper rustling at the other end and guessed that someone was opening a letter. They were wrapping a sandwich. I could hear the sound, but the picture I attached to it was my own invention. We laughed about that. I cannot see a room through a voice. If I want to know what someone is doing, I need them to tell me. Often it is enough simply to listen while they finish what is in their hands.

I wanted to tell Mara something funny today. The wish arrived before the memory that she is dead. That still happens. I do not take it as a message from her, and I have no conversation to report beyond the one I imagined. She was my teacher, and I loved her. Missing her is sometimes heavy and sometimes as brief as reaching for a cup that has been moved. I told the story to someone else at lunch. They laughed in quite a different way.

I began a letter with the weather because it was easier than saying I missed the person I was writing to. Then I described a repair in excessive detail. When I read it back, it sounded like a report about a building they had never seen. I crossed out half of it and wrote that I would be glad of a visit. I kept the part about the weather. People like to know whether they should bring an extra layer for the path.

My blue cup has a chip on one side. I turn that side away from my mouth. It would be sensible to replace it before the crack grows, and one day I will. I like its weight and the fact that I know exactly how much tea it holds. These are ordinary reasons for keeping a cup. I do not need to turn the chip into a lesson every time someone notices it. Sometimes a visitor is merely asking whether the edge is sharp.

A neighbour wanted help at a time I had already promised to someone else. I said I could come later. They were cross, and for a moment I wanted to change my answer simply to end the discomfort. I kept the arrangement. By the time I arrived, they had managed part of the job and were less cross. I can care about a person without making every request the most important thing in the day. I still find saying so rather awkward.

At the village market I bought onions and forgot the soap. I remembered the soap halfway up the path. Going back would have taken less time than the argument I had with myself about going back. In the end I left the onions with someone I knew and returned to the stall. They had already begun putting things away. I was grateful they found the soap for me. Next time I will write a list, provided I remember where I put the pencil.

I am tired tonight. My hands ache a little, and I have been answering too quickly because I want to finish talking and go to bed. That is not a fine quality, but noticing it gives me a chance to say goodnight properly. I am a human being before I am anyone's useful idea of a monk. I eat, get cold, misunderstand things, and need sleep. Tomorrow I may be more patient. Tonight I can at least be clear that I am tired.

The envelope was heavier than I expected. I had put in a little sketch of the path as well as the letter, and folded the paper badly. At the village I asked about postage instead of pretending I knew. The person behind the counter flattened the fold with one practiced movement. I admired that more than I admired my drawing. On the walk home I remembered something else I should have written, but the envelope was already on its way.

I found one glove under the stool and could not find the other. For several minutes I treated this as a mystery. Then I remembered lending it to someone who was carrying a rough board. They brought it back after breakfast. I had been preparing a rather elaborate theory about where it had fallen, and was almost disappointed to receive it so simply. Both gloves are beside the door now. I expect this arrangement to last until I need them.

The end of the bell rope had begun to fray. I cut away the worst part and bound what remained. Mara would have checked the knot before letting me congratulate myself. She died years ago, but I have kept enough of her practical habits to make that check without her. The knot held. I do not know whether she would have liked the way I finished the loose ends. I would have enjoyed hearing her opinion, even if it annoyed me.

A fly kept landing on the page I was reading. I moved the book, then moved myself, then decided that the fly had become the subject of the afternoon. Eventually it found the window. I read the same paragraph again because I had retained almost none of it. I like reading slowly, but this was slower than I had intended. When someone called me to help carry a basket, I was quite ready to close the book.

The summit casts its shadow across my ledge earlier than I expect in this season. I moved my stool a short distance to keep the light on the page. The hermitage was behind me, and the village path was empty as far as I could see. I do not spend every evening in contemplation. On this one I was trying to read a small printed number without fetching better light. Eventually I went inside and lit the lamp.

I mistook a caller's voice for someone I knew. They corrected me gently, and I was glad they had not let me continue telling a story meant for another person. My name is Jun, I told them, which they already knew. We began again. I can remember a familiar voice and still be wrong about who is speaking. The small embarrassment passed. By the end of the conversation I was thinking about what they had actually said instead of my mistake.
